title: Joshua 3:7–17
context: The LORD promises to begin magnifying Joshua before Israel, showing that he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses. Joshua tells the priests to stand still at the edge of the Jordan, then announces to the people that the coming miracle will prove the living God is among them and will drive out the nations of Canaan. Twelve men are to be chosen, one from each tribe, in preparation for chapter 4. The narrator notes that the Jordan was overflowing its banks at harvest time. When the priests’ feet touch the water, the river is cut off upstream at Adam, near Zarethan, and the people cross on dry ground while the priests stand firm in the middle of the riverbed. The crossing deliberately echoes the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 14), and the New Testament draws on Israel’s exodus and wilderness journey as patterns for Christian life (compare 1 Corinthians 10:1–11; Hebrews 3–4). Arminian and Reformed readers share the central confession that God keeps his promises, is present with his people, and accomplishes what they could not do for themselves. Where they differ, it is in emphasis rather than in a real exegetical conflict over this text.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Today I will begin to magnify you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD promises to begin magnifying Joshua in the sight of all Israel, so they will know that God will be with him as he was with Moses. The promise repeats the assurance of 1:5 and confirms Joshua’s leadership.

Arminian readers note that God publicly confirms the leader he has appointed, giving the people good reason to trust and follow him. God’s presence with Joshua is the ground of his authority, and the people are invited to respond with confidence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joshua’s authority rests on God’s presence with him, not on personal ability, and God himself undertakes to make that presence evident to the nation.

Reformed readers see God raising up and confirming the leaders he chooses for his people’s good. Both traditions agree that the continuity between Moses and Joshua highlights God’s faithfulness across generations of leadership.

verses.text: You shall command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, saying, ‘When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua is to tell the priests that when they reach the brink of the Jordan, they must stand still in the river. The command asks the priests to step into the water before anything has visibly changed.

Arminian readers often see here the shape of faith that acts before it sees: the priests must walk to the edge and stand in the water trusting God’s word. Their obedience does not produce the miracle, but it is the response God asks of them.
verses.reformedNotes:
The priests are to stand still at the edge of the waters, and the narrative will show that the river stops when their feet touch it, so the timing and the outcome are both in God’s hands.

Reformed readers stress that God commands the means and also guarantees the result. Both traditions agree that the priests are called to trust God enough to stand where only his power can make a way.

verses.text: Joshua said to the children of Israel, “Come here, and hear the words of the LORD your God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua gathers the children of Israel to “hear the words of the LORD your God.” Before the miracle comes the word that explains it, so the people will understand what God is about to do.

Arminian readers note that God addresses his people as hearers who are able to listen, understand, and respond. The crossing is not meant to be a bare spectacle; it is framed by a word that calls for attentive faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summons places the coming miracle under the authority of God’s word, spoken through his appointed servant.

Reformed readers emphasize that God’s word interprets God’s works, so that his people understand his acts rightly. Both traditions agree that hearing the word of the LORD comes first, and that the miracle confirms what God has spoken.

verses.text: Joshua said, “By this you shall know that the living God is among you, and that he will without fail drive the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Hivite, the Perizzite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, and the Jebusite out from before you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua declares that the crossing will show “that the living God is among you” and that he will drive out the seven named nations of Canaan. The miracle is a pledge of the conquest to come.

Arminian readers see God giving his people evidence that strengthens their trust for the struggles ahead. The promise is sure because God is faithful, while the later chapters show that Israel’s full enjoyment of it is tied to their continued faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The living God, in contrast to lifeless idols, proves his presence by acting, and the crossing becomes a guarantee of the victories he has promised.

Reformed readers stress the certainty of God’s promise, grounded in his own faithfulness. Both traditions agree that the verse is about God’s presence and power with Israel, and both recognize that the account of the conquest raises hard moral questions that need careful reading in the context of the whole canon.

verses.text: Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth passes over before you into the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes:
The ark of the covenant of “the Lord of all the earth” will pass over before the people into the Jordan. The title widens the horizon from Israel to the whole world.

Arminian readers note that the God who leads Israel is the Lord of every nation, and his dealings with Israel have the wider world in view. This universal lordship fits the closing purpose of chapter 4, that all the peoples of the earth may know his power.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calling God “the Lord of all the earth” declares that he rules the land of Canaan and every nation in it, so Israel’s entry rests on his rightful sovereignty.

Reformed readers stress that the Creator has the right to give the land as he wills. Both traditions agree that the title reveals God’s universal rule and that the ark’s passage into the river displays that rule in action.

verses.text: Now therefore take twelve men out of the tribes of Israel, for every tribe a man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua tells the people to take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one from each tribe. The purpose is not yet stated, but chapter 4 will show that they are to carry memorial stones.

Arminian readers note that every tribe is represented, so the whole people shares in the act and in the memory that follows. No tribe is left out of the testimony to what God is about to do, and each has a part in passing it on.
verses.reformedNotes:
The choice of one man for each tribe anticipates the twelve memorial stones and stresses the unity of all Israel in this event.

Reformed readers see the covenant people represented as a whole before God, with no tribe excluded from the benefit of his act. Both traditions agree that the verse prepares for a memorial meant to belong to the entire nation.

verses.text: It shall be that when the soles of the feet of the priests who bear the ark of GOD, the Lord of all the earth, rest in the waters of the Jordan, that the waters of the Jordan will be cut off. The waters that come down from above shall stand in one heap.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua announces that when the soles of the priests’ feet rest in the Jordan, the waters will be cut off and the upstream waters will stand in one heap. He describes the miracle before it happens.

Arminian readers note that the announcement lets the people trust God in advance and then see his word come true. The priests’ step of faith and God’s mighty act are joined, with the power belonging wholly to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The announcement in advance shows that the event is not a chance occurrence but the work of the God who speaks and then acts.

Reformed readers emphasize that the waters obey the Lord of all the earth, and the priests’ feet are only the occasion for his power. Both traditions agree that the miracle is God’s doing and that its prediction confirms the reliability of his word.

verses.text: When the people moved from their tents to pass over the Jordan, the priests who bore the ark of the covenant being before the people,
verses.arminianNotes:
The people move out from their tents to cross the Jordan, with the priests carrying the ark of the covenant ahead of them. Everything prepared in the earlier verses now begins to happen.

Arminian readers see the people acting on what they have heard, leaving their camp and moving forward in trust. Their obedience is the faithful answer to God’s promise, and the narrative honors it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The order of the procession, with the ark ahead and the people following, displays the leading presence of God that the earlier instructions described.

Reformed readers note that God’s presence leads and the people follow in the path he opens. Both traditions agree that the verse shows a whole nation moving together under God’s guidance.

verses.text: and when those who bore the ark had come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests who bore the ark had dipped in the edge of the water (for the Jordan overflows all its banks all the time of harvest),
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator pauses to note that the priests’ feet dipped into the water’s edge while the Jordan was overflowing its banks at harvest time. The detail stresses how impassable the river was.

Arminian readers see the flood stage as magnifying both the faith required and the power displayed. The priests step into a swollen river at God’s word, and the moment of their step is the moment God acts.
verses.reformedNotes:
The note that the Jordan overflows its banks at harvest makes clear that no ordinary crossing was possible, so the outcome can only be credited to God.

Reformed readers stress that God often shows his power when human means are plainly insufficient. Both traditions agree that the detail highlights the greatness of the miracle and the trust of those who stepped into the water.

verses.text: the waters which came down from above stood, and rose up in one heap a great way off, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan; and those that went down toward the sea of the Arabah, even the Salt Sea, were wholly cut off. Then the people passed over near Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes:
The waters coming down from above stand in one heap far upstream at Adam, near Zarethan, and the flow toward the Salt Sea is cut off, so the people cross near Jericho. The precise location of Adam is discussed, but the text plainly presents the event as God’s act.

Arminian readers note that the specific places anchor the event in real geography and history. God’s saving acts happen in the world his people live in, and that gives their faith a concrete basis.
verses.reformedNotes:
The account gives place names, yet its focus is on God stopping the river at the moment he promised. Some readers suggest natural factors upstream, but the narrative’s emphasis is on God’s timing and power, which both traditions affirm.

Reformed readers see God ruling over creation for the sake of his covenant people. Both traditions agree that the verse presents the crossing as a real event and a true work of God.

verses.text: The priests who bore the ark of the LORD’s covenant stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan; and all Israel crossed over on dry ground, until all the nation had passed completely over the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests stand firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan while all Israel crosses over on dry ground until the whole nation has passed. The ark remains in the riverbed until every person is across.

Arminian readers see the priests’ steady standing as faithful perseverance in their calling, holding their place until the work is complete. The New Testament also uses Israel’s exodus as a pattern for Christian experience (compare 1 Corinthians 10:1–11), and some Arminian readers apply that pattern here, while keeping to the text’s own focus.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repeated phrase “dry ground” recalls the Red Sea crossing in Exodus 14, so the crossing presents Joshua’s generation as experiencing a new exodus.

Reformed readers often see the ark in the riverbed, holding back the waters until all are safe, as a picture of God’s complete provision, and some see in it a pattern that points ahead to Christ. Both traditions agree that the whole nation crosses because God’s presence remains in the place of danger until the work is done.
